findings.title: SQL built by string concatenation/interpolation (heuristic)
findings.explanation: A SQL statement appears to be assembled from variables instead of bound parameters. If any part is user-controlled this allows SQL injection. This is a pattern match only - it has NOT been confirmed as exploitable.
findings.remediation: Use parameterised queries / prepared statements or the ORM's query builder.

findings.title: Transport encryption / certificate validation disabled
findings.explanation: The connection to a non-local host disables TLS or certificate validation, exposing credentials and data to interception.
findings.remediation: Enable TLS (e.g. sslmode=require/verify-full, Encrypt=True) and validate server certificates.

findings.title: Multiple database technologies detected
findings.evidence: MySQL, Oracle Database, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, MongoDB
findings.explanation: Evidence for several databases was found: MySQL, Oracle Database, PostgreSQL, Microsoft SQL Server, MongoDB. This is normal for polyglot systems but worth confirming (e.g. SQLite in tests, PostgreSQL in production).
findings.remediation: Confirm which database each environment uses.

findings.title: MongoDB: driver used but no connection configuration found
findings.explanation: The code imports a database driver but no connection string, provider setting or config keys were found in the scanned files. Configuration may be supplied at deployment (environment variables, secret store) or be missing.
findings.remediation: Document the required settings (e.g. in .env.example) and verify them in the target environment.

limitations: Static text analysis only: no project code is executed and no database connection is ever attempted.
'confirmed' means explicit configuration was found - not that the database is reachable, that credentials work, or that the code path is exercised at runtime.
Comments are skipped using simple per-language rules; string literals and docstrings are not distinguished from code, so a connection string inside a docstring can still be reported.
Files larger than the configured size limit, binary files (except SQLite file headers), and third-party folders (node_modules, venv, vendor, bin/obj, ...) are not scanned.
Dialect detection from SQL keywords is heuristic; ORM entity discovery covers common patterns only.
SQLite/SQL Server data files are detected by name/header but their contents are never opened or parsed.
